findings.title: Generosity as productive care
findings.claim: The focus's Rabb and al-Akram relation can be heard as productive care: reading and teaching become a rain-like provision that carries dependent capacity toward knowledge.
findings.mechanism: Rabb B002 supplies staged development while al-Akram B001 supplies praiseworthy generosity and B002 supplies fertile growth; teaching and recitation connections make the cultivation image contact the focus words.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader receives the command to read as an enabled act whose capacity is itself generously cultivated, rather than as a self-generated performance.
findings.containment: The reading remains bounded by the local Lord-title and superlative generosity; it uses the rain and fertility image only to clarify developmental provision, not to activate unrelated agricultural branches.

epistemic.reason: A trusted publication supports the branch pairing, while the wider cultivation contact is an interpretive resonance and the connection targets lack supplied morphology.

findings.title: Generous gift and responsible return
findings.claim: The generous gift remains gratuitous while creating a relation of responsible return: what the Rabb gives is not owned as autonomous self-possession, and the return to Him becomes the recipient's answer.
findings.mechanism: Rabb B001 joins lordship and ownership to al-Akram B001's noble generosity, while al-Akram B008 supplies a bounded return-and-recompense contact; gratitude, accountability, and provision connections activate the relation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can receive reading and knowledge as gift without reducing generosity to payment, while recognizing that reception has an accountable direction.
findings.containment: The return relation is ethical and answerable, not a commercial exchange; B008 is used only as a constrained contact with expected response and does not replace B001's non-reductive generosity.

epistemic.reason: The trusted finding explicitly supplies the gift-and-return claim; the broader contextual contacts qualify its scope without changing the local lexical floor.

findings.title: Generosity beyond human sufficiency
findings.claim: Al-Akram makes the human claim to sufficiency an unequal contest: divine generosity is the measure against which human attempts to establish superiority or self-sufficiency fail.

findings.reader_payoff: The reader's status claims are displaced by a prior standard of generosity that cannot be matched through boasting or possession.
findings.containment: The contest is limited to generosity and its value-order; it does not activate every rivalry, rank, or material-wealth image available elsewhere.

epistemic.reason: The trusted publication states the superiority-contest claim and the selected connections support its human-sufficiency contrast.
